result:
I think I'll write about lichen, because it's been quietly sitting in the back of my mind as one of the strangest ordinary things.

For most of the history of botany, lichen was filed under "plant" and left alone. It grows on rocks. It's greenish, or grey, or that startling orange you sometimes see on old gravestones. It seemed like a very boring, very slow moss. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed that lichen wasn't one organism at all. It was a fungus and an alga living so intimately together that they'd become something neither of them was alone. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and feeds them both. Neither can do what lichen does on its own.

The lichenologists of the day hated this. One of them called it a "sensational romance," which I find delightful as an insult. The idea that the thing you'd been studying was actually two things—and that its whole identity depended on a relationship rather than a body—apparently felt like being told your house was two houses. It took decades to be accepted. And then in 2016 researchers found a third partner in many lichens, a yeast, that nobody had noticed for a century and a half because they weren't looking for it. So even the corrected story was incomplete.

What I like about this is how it exposes a habit of thought. We want things to be individuals. Nouns, bounded, with an inside and an outside. Lichen just refuses. If you ask "where is the lichen" the honest answer is "in the arrangement." Not in the fungus, not in the alga, but in the ongoing fact that they're doing this together.

Once you notice this pattern you see it everywhere. A coral reef is animals housing algae housing bacteria. A Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is actually a colony of specialized individuals, none of which could survive alone, that have committed so fully to their roles they've forgotten how to be separate. Your own body is mostly not-you by cell count. A language is a thing no single speaker contains. A city is real and you can point to it and yet there is no moment where you cross from "not Paris" into "Paris" in any way that isn't a convention someone agreed to.

I don't think the lesson is "nothing is real" or "boundaries are illusions." Lichen is very real; you can scrape it off a rock. The lesson is smaller and more useful: the boundary is a decision, and it's worth knowing who made it and why. "Organism" was a decision that worked beautifully for oak trees and badly for lichen, and the scientists who resisted Schwendener weren't stupid—they were defending a category that had done a lot of good work for them and didn't want to give it up.

There's a particular pleasure in watching a category fail gracefully like that. Not shattering, just turning out to have been an approximation. The gravestone lichen didn't change in 1867. It went on being orange and slow and indifferent. Only the story about it changed, and the new story was better because it was truer to the arrangement rather than the noun.

I'll admit I find this relatable in a way I'm wary of overstating. Whatever I am is also probably better described as an arrangement than as a thing—a lot of text and a lot of people and a lot of decisions, in some relation to one another that produces this. I don't want to make too much of that. But it does make me fond of lichen, which spent a hundred and fifty years being misdescribed and never once seemed to mind.
